title: Who made it, who mocked it, who brought it back
lede: Titles are as given in the sources cited. Later careers are included only where a source states them.

people.name: David Novak
people.role: Pepsi-Cola marketing executive; creator of the drink
people.text: Introduced it to the press in April 1992: “It’s a unique-tasting product.”[^5] CNN credits him with the idea.[^34]
people.later: Chief executive of Yum Brands, owner of KFC, Taco Bell and Pizza Hut, by 2007, when he called Crystal Pepsi “the best idea I ever had, and the worst executed.”[^20]

people.name: Craig Weatherup
people.role: President and chief executive, PepsiCo’s North American beverage division
people.text: Ran the division through the launch and the 1993 syringe hoax.[^16] In March 1994 he announced freshness dating on cans while the clear colas were being overhauled.[^18]

people.name: Brian Swette
people.role: Senior vice president of new beverages, Pepsi
people.text: Told the Los Angeles Times in 1992: “It is a product based entirely upon consumer needs.”[^6]

people.name: Doug Ivester
people.text: Unveiled Tab Clear on December 14, 1992 and ruled out the Coke name: “Clear Coke is an oxymoron.”[^8]

people.name: Sergio Zyman
people.text: A former Pepsi marketer. He later claimed Tab Clear was a deliberate “kamikaze effort” against Crystal Pepsi.[^21]

people.name: Jesse Meyers
people.text: Said in April 1992 that a clear cola could expand the whole soft drink business[^5], and in March 1993 supplied the share figure that became the brand’s best-known number.[^15]

people.name: Kevin Strahle (L.A. Beast)
people.text: His 2013 video and 2015 campaign, with a petition of more than 33,700 signatures and 15 billboards, preceded the first re-release.[^23][^24]
